# Abstract {.unnumbered}

<!-- RAP 2 (tax rates), findings in chapter order; adapted from the JMP abstract (JMP/paper.qmd). Previous version: Thesis/feedback/thesis-abstract-intro-archive-250926.md -->

Sales and value-added taxes that credit purchases reward firms for overreporting their inputs: every fictitious dollar of deductible inputs lowers their tax liability, and the higher the rate, the larger the reward. How this evasion responds to the tax rate is largely unknown, because true inputs are not observed and firms that overreport may be mistaken for low-productivity firms. This thesis separates overreporting from productivity using the production function, with corporations, which government and market scrutiny keep from evading, as the truth-reporting benchmark. The approach needs only reported inputs and output, so it applies equally to standard firm-level surveys and administrative data; I apply it to Colombian manufacturing firms from 1981 to 1991. First, a statistical test, valid for any detection probability, evasion cost and common technology, and whose rejections can only point to overreporting, detects overreporting in 9 of 20 industries, including four of the five largest. Second, deconvolution recovers its distribution: in the five industries where the test rejects at the 1% level, firms overreport on average between 11% and 25% of their true materials. Third, correcting for overreporting yields consistently smaller output elasticities of materials and less dispersed, more persistent productivity, with a 90–10 ratio about 40% lower and a half-life of productivity shocks two to seven times longer. Fourth, after a 1983 reform raised the sales-tax rate in most industries, overreporting by unincorporated firms in the affected industries rose, reaching about 9% of true materials by 1987. Finally, a structural model of detection and evasion costs shows that a 0.5% increase in the sales-tax rate raises claimed deductions by between 16% and 28%, far more than its mechanical effect, while cuts lower them only gradually: the smallest cut statistically distinguishable from current policy is 8%.
